processes: Predicting behavior from a group number
Connecting group position to valence electrons
plainLanguageExplanation: A group is a vertical column of the periodic table. The elements in a column — one above another — are called a group, and they are grouped together for a very good reason: they behave alike. The members of a group share the same number of valence electrons, which is the number of electrons in their outermost shell. Since valence electrons decide how atoms bond and react, elements with the same count act in similar ways. For example, Group 1 (the alkali metals) all have one valence electron, and they are all soft, shiny, and famously reactive. Group 18 (the noble gases) all have full outer shells, and they are all famously unreactive. Because of this, the group number is one of the most useful predictions in chemistry: find an element's column and you already know a lot about how it will behave. Columns are numbered 1 through 18 across the table (older tables also use labels like IA, IIA...).

whyItMatters: The group is the periodic table's built-in crystal ball. Because column-mates share valence electrons and behavior, knowing an element's group lets you predict how reactive it is, what kinds of bonds it forms, and even what compounds it is likely to make — without ever having touched the element.
didYouKnow: Because elements in the same group act alike, chemists can predict a brand-new element's behavior from its column before they have even created a sample of it.
compareReason: Groups (columns) and periods (rows) are the two directions the table is organized by — comparing them shows that columns group behavior while rows count shells.
